newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Japan maintains claim to islets disputed with China.
newsitem.headline: Japan maintains claim to islets disputed with China.

text.p: Japan has sent a letter to Secretary-General Kofi Annan maintaining its claim to the disputed Senkaku Islands, which China also claims under the name Diaoyu.

In the letter, made public on Monday, Japanese U.N. envoy Hisashi Owada said that, since a letter from China stating its claim had been made an addendum to a U.N. report on the law of the sea, Japan wanted its letter also included as an addendum.

"In view of the history of the Senkaku Islands and in the light of the relevant principles of international law, there is no question that the islands are an integral part of the territory of Japan, and that Japan has always exercised effective control over them. It is thus the position of the government of Japan that no question of territorial title should arise with respect to those islands," Owada said.
Chinese U.N. envoy Qin Huasun, in a letter to the secretary-general last December, also took issue with the way the dispute was referred to in the U.N. report.
The lengthy report, issued last November, made only a brief reference to the dispute as one of several involving rival maritime claims.

China's note said that "Diaoyu Island and all the islands appertaining thereto have been part of China's territory since ancient times, which has been justified by historical facts and international law."
Qin also objected to the report's describing the islands as under Japan's "effective control," since he said that term carried a specific meaning under international law.

China added that the islands were located "about 92 miles northeast of Jilong City of China's Taiwan province" and it objected to the report's saying they were located "about 200 miles east of the Chinese coast," since that "could be understood as excluding China's Taiwan Province from the Chinese territory."

It dismissed the report's suggestion that the main reason so much attention had been focused on the islands was because surveys had suggested the presence nearby of large oil reserves. China said the real reason was "the provocative actions by a group of Japanese right-wingers who set up a lighthouse and a Japanese flag on the islands of Japan" last July.
